title: Stochastic thermodynamics and predictability of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes: an application to the Madden-Julian Oscillation
authors: Roberta Benincasa, Danni Du, Gregory S. Duane, Jeffrey B. Weiss
abstract: Climate oscillations are intrinsically out-of-equilibrium phenomena, yet the connection between their predictability and nonequilibrium thermodynamic properties remains unexplored. We develop a coarse-grained stochastic thermodynamic framework for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) processes and apply this framework to climate data via linear inverse models (LIMs), linking predictability, entropy production, dynamical activity, and path action. Climate oscillations are often studied in a 2d phase space of climate indices, which are even under time-reversal, motivating our focus on 2d OU dynamics with even variables. We find that coordinate-invariant properties of 2d OU processes can be reduced to a minimal three-parameter description: two diffusivities and a phase-space rotation. We show that these quantities fundamentally characterize distinct aspects of the dynamics. We find that higher irreversibility and dynamical activity do not necessarily imply reduced predictability. Rather, it is the path action which is most closely connected to a commonly used measure of predictability, the anomaly correlation coefficient (ACC). As an illustrative example, we apply this framework to the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) over the twentieth century. We find that the MJO has become simultaneously more predictable, as seen previously, while at the same time becoming more irreversible and more active. Predictability is driven predominantly by the reduced mean diffusion. Entropy production reflects the combined evolution of all three parameters. These results suggest that stochastic thermodynamics provides a powerful lens for studying nonequilibrium climate phenomena.
summary: This paper links climate predictability to nonequilibrium thermodynamics by developing a stochastic framework for OU processes. It shows that for systems like the MJO, predictability is governed by the path action, even when other thermodynamic measures like irreversibility increase. This suggests stochastic thermodynamics offers a powerful lens for analyzing complex, out-of-equilibrium geophysical phenomena.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental connection between the predictability of out-of-equilibrium climate oscillations and their underlying nonequilibrium thermodynamic properties.
main_result: The path action, rather than irreversibility or dynamical activity, is found to be the most direct predictor of forecast skill (ACC) for systems like the MJO. The MJO exhibits increased predictability alongside increased irreversibility and activity.
method: The authors develop and apply a coarse-grained stochastic thermodynamic framework to Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) processes, analyzing their dynamics using concepts like entropy production and path action.
model_or_system: The model uses the multivariate OU stochastic differential equation, focusing on 2D dynamics with even variables, and applies this framework to analyze climate indices, specifically the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO).
key_observables: Predictability (Anomaly Correlation Coefficient, ACC), Entropy Production ($\sigma$), Dynamical Activity ($\phi$), and Path Action ($\alpha$).
important_parameters: Two diffusivities and a phase-space rotation characterize the coordinate-invariant dynamics of the 2D OU process.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to 2D OU dynamics with even variables, and the framework treats climate change as a succession of steady-states.
paper_structure: The paper first develops the stochastic thermodynamic framework for OU processes, then analyzes the reduced parameter space using coordinate-invariant properties, and finally applies the entire methodology to the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO).
why_interesting: The application of fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics to macroscopic, non-equilibrium systems like climate dynamics provides a powerful theoretical tool for understanding predictability limits in complex physical systems.
